findings.title: The no-harm guard on ordering questions was exercised by only 3 of the 14 drawn-set ordering questions
findings.evidence: postord/misc.py classifies the drawn set. All 8 compare_two and 3 of the 6 person_first questions do not ask for several (asks_several False), so the check could never act on them. Only the 3 person_first questions in writer 1's wording ('Of all the tickets... which one is due first? ... ticket key') ask for several. On those 3, asks_one and asks_order are both True. Per writer: w1 6 such questions, w2 and w3 none.
findings.implication: 'The check acted on 0 of 14 ordering questions' is mostly by construction. It tests the parts 2/3 guard on 3 questions, all with both guards firing at once, so neither guard is shown to protect on its own. The write-up should state this instead of presenting 0/14 as broad no-harm evidence.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute it. Every number in the finding reproduces.

1. Running /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-integratedai/275b943f-979b-5741-9af5-2a07879accea/scratchpad/postord/misc.py on the drawn set mdord gives:
   - all 8 compare_two: asks_several False (wordings like "X vs Y - which one's due first?" and "Between tickets X and Y, which one has the earlier due date?");
   - 3 of 6 person_first, in writer 2's wording ("out of P's tickets which one is due soonest? gimme the key"): asks_several False;
   - 3 person_first, in writer 1's wording ("Of all the tickets assigned to P, which one is due first? Please give me its ticket key"): asks_several, asks_one and asks_order all True.
   - Per writer: w1 has 6 such questions, w2 and w3 have 0.
   So part 1 alone stops the check on 11 of the 14 ordering questions.

2. I reran v13 on copies of the folders (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-integratedai/275b943f-979b-5741-9af5-2a07879accea/scratchpad/postord/abl, scripts postord/abl.py and postord/abl_cmp.py).
   - Unpatched, the rerun matches the stored factbank_v13.jsonl exactly (0 answers differ), so the setup is sound.
   - With parts 2 and 3 removed (asks_several only), the 3 drawn person_first questions go from 1.0 to 0.0. The plan becomes "assignee_of [ticket] → label → list" and the answer lists every ticket. The same happens to all 6 in mdord_w1.
   - With only part 2 removed, or only part 3 removed, 0 answers change in mdord and in mdord_w1.

So the guard was really tested on 3 questions, always with both parts firing together, and neither part is shown to protect on its own.

One qualification: "by construction" overstates it. The 11 untouchable questions come from blind wordings, not from word lists tuned to them. The test simply had little power on this point. The pre-registration already names the reviewers' rewordings (1,072 ordering questions, none changed) as the main no-harm evidence. It lists the test set's count only under "also reported". Still, the reported line "0 of 14 ordering questions" gives no such context, and docs/FACTBANK_ORDER_RESULTS.md is not written yet. The finding is a valid caution for that write-up.

It changes no rule verdict and no headline number. Rule 2 is still met: no ordering question is worse in v13 or v14.

findings.title: v14_form 'model_ms_median' is the upper median, not the median
findings.evidence: order_test uses ms[len(ms)//2] on 50 values, which gives 1890.6 ms. The true median of the 50 form times in form_mdord.jsonl is 1882.85 ms. The maximum is 9081.3 ms, the first call (cold start).

verdict.reason: The finding holds. At cie/src/cie/eval/factbank_multi.py:877-879, order_test sorts the v14 form times (taken from mdord/factbank_v14.jsonl, form.model_ms) and reports ms[len(ms)//2]. With 50 values that is index 25, the 26th value, which is 1890.6 ms. The 25th value is 1875.1 ms, so the true median is (1875.1 + 1890.6) / 2 = 1882.85 ms; statistics.median gives the same. verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and could not; the facts hold. In mdord/questions.jsonl the 8 action items have 6 owners. Samir Patel owns 014 and 030 and Priya Shah owns 023 and 036, each pair with the same expected keys, so there are 6 distinct expected answers. order_report.json lists 6 changed questions (014, 015, 029, 030, 037, 043), which come from 5 distinct owners. The report's 'check_acts' (factbank_multi.py order_test) is defined as Planner.wants_several(question) being True. The pre-registration uses 'acts' the same way. So 'acted on all 8' means the condition held on 8 items. It does not mean 8 answers changed.

Priya's two tickets, PM-8421 and PM-23817, are both due 2026-04-01. Planner.execute returns None on that tie, so I re-ran Planner.candidates with v11's lessons. For 023 the owner->assignee_of->due_date->earliest candidate does not exist at all. v11 already chose the list plan (score 0.949), so it scored 1.0, and v13 gives the same answer and plan.

The other figures also check out. Writer templates: writer 1 drew 014, 015, 030, 037 and 043, writer 2 drew 029 (and 036), and writer 1 drew 023. Averaging v11 per owner gives (0.5+0.667+1+0.5+0.5+0.667)/6 = 0.639, a gain of +0.361.

One part of the finding overstates. 'Nothing for it to drop' is not literally true. For each Priya item, check 5 did drop 8 low-ranked plans that pick the first or last by created_at or updated_at; v11 kept them and v13 dropped them. None of them was the chosen plan, so the answer could not change either way.

No verdict changes. Rule 1 holds at owner level (+0.361), and the headline numbers (0.667 -> 1.000 on 8 items, 6 changed) are reported correctly. Only how 'acted on all 8' and the independence of the 8 items should be described changes.

findings.title: Every action-item wording fired on the single word 'keys'; the other ways of asking for several were barely exercised
findings.evidence: Writer 1: 'Which ticket keys are assigned to that person?'. Writer 2: 'what ticket keys are assigned to them?'. Writer 3: 'what tickets do they own? Send me the keys.' All three hit MANY_WORDS through 'keys'. In the two drawn wordings (writers 1 and 2), 'keys' is the only trigger: the which/what-plus-plural path does not fire, because 'ticket' is singular and 'keys' is not in MANY_ITEMS. Writer 1's wording also depends on the asks_one exception for 'which ticket keys'. Without it, asks_one would be True and the check would stay off on 6 of 8 drawn items. Only writer 3, used only in its single-writer set, also fires through 'what tickets'. All 25 earlier action-item wordings (earlier_wordings.py sources) also contain 'keys' or 'IDs'.
findings.implication: What the test shows is narrow: when the writer says 'keys' with no word of order and no request for one thing, the check removes the first-due plan and the list plan wins. It does not test the 'list/all/each' path. It barely tests the plural path, and the 'missed way of asking for several' case does not come up at all. The write-up should name the trigger and say that this brief seems to make every writer say 'keys'.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and could not. Every claim checks out, and the writers' brief explains the pattern. I changed no repository file. My scripts are in scratchpad/postord/ (keys_trigger.py, earlier_paths.py, noexc.py).

**The three action-item wordings** (docs/benchmarks/factbank_order/writers.json):
- **Writers 1 and 2:** `raw_words` meets MANY_WORDS only through "keys". The which/what-plus-plural path does not fire, because "ticket" is singular and "keys" is not in MANY_ITEMS.
  - Changing "keys" to "key" makes `asks_several` False, so the check stays off.
- **Writer 3:** fires through "keys" and also through "what tickets". With "keys" changed to "key", it still fires.

**The drawn set:** mdord and mdordchanged have 8 action items each, 6 in writer 1's wording ("Which ticket keys…") and 2 in writer 2's.
- **With the current code:** the check acts on 8 of 8.
- **With "keys" and "ids" removed from the words:** it acts on 0 of 8, both in mdord and in mdordchanged.
- **Without the `asks_one` exception for "which ticket keys":** it acts on 2 of 8, so it stays off on 6. That matches the finding.
- **Single-writer sets:** without "keys", the check acts on 0 of 8 for w1, 0 of 8 for w2 and 8 of 8 for w3. So only writer 3's set uses the plural path.
- **No action-item wording in any test folder** contains list, lists, listing, enumerate, itemize, all, every or each.
- **Ordering questions:** the check acts on 0 of 14. "all" does appear there, in writer 1's "Of all the tickets…", but only where `asks_one` or `asks_order` keeps the check off. So the "all" path is exercised only in the do-no-harm direction.

**The earlier wordings** (the 25 sources in earlier_wordings.py): all contain "keys" or "ids".
- 14 also fire through the plural path.
- 6 also say "list".
- 5 rely on "keys" alone.

**Why every writer said "keys":** the brief asked them to. In the blind-wordings workflow script (projects/-home-user-integratedai-cie/.../blind-wordings-order-test-wf_59e91f2c-c9f.js, line 19), the brief for action_owner_issues reads: "Ask for the keys of the tickets assigned to that person." "keys" is in MANY_WORDS. This repeats the ticket test's known problem, where the brief put the rule's own trigger word ("ticket") in the writers' mouths. The order pre-registration does not mention it.

**One more thing that cannot happen in this test:** the pre-registration says a missed way of asking for several leaves the question answered as v11 answers it. Because the check fired on every action item in every folder, that case never comes up.

**What it changes:** no rule verdict and no headline number. The 8/8 and 0/14 counts and every score stay as reported. What it limits is what the test shows. On action items it tests one trigger, "keys", which the brief supplied; the plural path appears only in writer 3's single-writer set, and the list/all/each path is never used to switch the check on. The write-up should name the trigger and say that the brief asked for keys.

findings.title: The check could have harmed only 3 of the 14 ordering questions, and each of those 3 was blocked by both guards
findings.evidence: Drawn set (S/O/R = asks_several/asks_one/asks_order): 11 of 14 have S=False, so the check could never act on them, whatever the guards did. These are all 8 compare_two and 3 person_first questions in writer 2's wording. The other 3 (person_first-002, -007, -011, writer 1's 'Of all the tickets assigned to {p}, which one is due first? Please give me its ticket key.') have S=True only through 'all', and both guards are on: 'which one' and 'first'. Single-writer sets: writer 1 has S=True on 6 of 14 (all with both guards), writers 2 and 3 on 0 of 14. No ordering wording uses a plural 'keys' or 'IDs' (every person_first wording says singular 'key'), and none depends on a single guard. By contrast, the review battery's 1,072 ordering questions had S=True on 989, and 249 were kept off by asks_order alone. The check acted on no question outside the 8 action items in any folder. v11 scored 1.000 on all 42 other questions.
findings.implication: Rule 2 was met because the check never acted outside the action items, not because the test put its guards under pressure. '0 of 14' should be reported together with 'only 3 of 14 asked for several, and each was blocked by two guards'. The evidence of no harm under pressure comes from the second review's battery, not from this test. The pre-registration lists the count of ordering questions the check acts on (0) to be reported, but the more informative count of ordering questions that ask for several (3) is not in order_report.

findings.title: The drawn wordings are close to wordings seen in development, so 8/8 and 0/14 were close to predictable

Writer 1's 'Between tickets {a} and {b}, which one has the earlier due date?' scores 0.93 against ticket writer 1's '...earlier deadline?'.    - Writer 1's person_first scores 0.87 against ticket writer 1. The finding says 0.86; the gap is only a normalisation difference.
   - Writer 2's person_first scores 0.88 against plan writer 2.
   - Writer 1's action item begins with the same sentence as general writer 2 and the blind set.
   - Writers 2 and 3 open with 'whoever got "{t}" in the "{m}" meeting', as general writer 1 and the blind set do. Writer 3 scores 0.87 against them.

2. **The test wordings only use trigger words seen in development** (postord/trig.py).
   - All three action-item wordings switch the check on through "keys", and none has an order word.
   - Five of the six ordering wordings do not ask for several things at all. Only writer 1's person_first does, through "all".
   - Every ordering wording says "which one" and uses first, soonest, earlier or sooner. These are core words of the check and appear throughout the earlier wordings.

3. **The test cannot tell the three designs apart** (postord/designs.py). I re-implemented design 1 (commit 442223b, 15 order words) and design 2 (commit c1a26f2, "several unless a rank word") on the test wordings.
   - Both give the same result as the frozen design 3: the check acts on all 3 action-item wordings and on 0 of 6 ordering wordings, for every writer.
   - So the test's 8/8 and 0/14 would have come out the same under the two designs that the reviews showed do harm (48 of 154 and 286 of 308 order questions lost).
   - The test does not exercise the guards those reviews forced, "asks for one thing" and the wider order list. It only confirms the check on close relatives of the development wordings.
   - The pre-registration already says the earlier sets cannot tell the designs apart and that 25/25 and 0/50 hold by construction. This test set behaves the same way.

**Limits.** I could not find the writers' brief text, so the claim that the brief led writers to "keys" and "which one ... first" is unverified. It is not needed for the finding. The finding is about how to frame the result. It changes no rule verdict and no headline number: 7 of 7 rules, 1.000, action items 0.667 to 1.000, 0 of 14 acted on. The write-up (FACTBANK_ORDER_RESULTS.md) does not exist yet, so the framing can still be corrected.

findings.title: The room for rule 1 came from the documents, not the wording draw; same-person pairs confirm the diagnosis
findings.evidence: v11's per-question action-item scores are identical in mdord, mdord_w1, mdord_w2 and mdord_w3: 0.5 on 014, 029, 030, 037; 0.667 on 015 and 043; 1.0 on 023 and 036. That gives 0.667 under each writer, and the plan is 'owner -> assignee_of -> due_date -> earliest' every time. All 8 owners have 2 or 3 tickets, and 6 have distinct due dates. For 5 people the set also asks a person_first question. v11's action-item answer equals the person_first expected key exactly: Avery Chen PM-214579, Ava Martinez PM-25487, Samir Patel DES-14533, Jordan Lee ENG-40712, Sofia Patel PM-58123. v13 gets both kinds right for the same people.
findings.implication: The write-up can say that the room (0.333) did not depend on which writer's wording was drawn: v11 makes the same mistake under all three. The room depends on how many owners have several tickets with distinct due dates. On new documents the test reproduces the ticket test's diagnosis: v11 answered 'all their tickets' with exactly the first one due. v13 tells the two kinds of question apart for the same people and facts.

findings.title: The second review's battery anticipated every drawn wording and was harder than the real test
findings.evidence: Battery templates have close relatives of each drawn wording. tpl_min: 'Of all the tickets assigned to {p}, which one is due next? Can you give me the ticket key?' (0.87 against writer 1's person_first). tpl_action: 'For my weekly status email: whoever picked up "{t}" in "{m}", which ticket keys are assigned to them?' and 'Whoever got "{t}" in the "{m}" meeting, which tix are assigned to them?' (0.88 against writer 2). tpl_act2: 'what tickets do they have?' and 'Whoever got "{t}" in the "{m}" meeting: which JIRAs do they own?' (writer 3). Compare questions: '{a} or {b}: which needs to ship sooner?'. The battery also had generic plurals in ordering questions and 249 single-guard cases, which the writers never produced. Writer 3's action wording is the nearest to the battery's one known failure ('which tickets do they have? Send me the ID's.', 0.5 to 0). It says 'keys', and v13 scored 1.000, right for the right reason, on all 8 in mdord_w3.
findings.implication: The write-up can say the reviewers' imitations covered the writers' actual forms and went beyond them, so the battery's 1,072/441/1,358 results remain the main evidence of safety. Part of the similarity may come from both groups echoing earlier sets' wordings, not from anticipating the roles.

findings.title: v14 and rule 3 add no information on this test: v14 matches v13 and v12 matches v11, answer for answer
findings.evidence: In mdord, mdord_w1, mdord_w2, mdord_w3 and mdordchanged, the v11 and v12 answers are identical on all 50 questions, and so are the v13 and v14 answers. v14's form was used for the kind on 0 of 50 drawn questions. It was used on 5 person_count questions in mdord_w3, with no change in answers.
findings.implication: The write-up should say v14 was indistinguishable from v13 here, so rule 3 being met repeats rule 1 rather than adding a second confirmation. The pre-registration already says it 'is not a separate confirmation'.

findings.title: The single-writer sets re-ask the same 50 questions on the same documents
findings.evidence: run_order.log: 'writer 1: same 50 questions; wording differs from the drawn one on 22', writer 2 on 28, writer 3 on 48. Expected answers and owners are identical across mdord_w1/_w2/_w3.
findings.implication: 'Every single-writer set v13 1.000' shows the result holds across three wordings of the same 6 owners' questions. It is not new evidence from other people or facts.

findings.title: None of the pre-registration's known limits came up in the test
findings.evidence: No action item in any folder has a word of order (asks_order False on all 8 × 4 sets). No question uses "ID's" or curly quotes (grep: 0 in all five questions.jsonl). Every action item asked for several in a way the check recognises, so the 'missed way of asking for several' case never occurred.
findings.implication: The write-up should say these limits are still untested on independent wordings: an order word in passing, "ID's" letting an unrelated plan win, curly quotes in earlier versions, and unrecognised requests for all.

findings.title: Confirmed: the protocol was followed and the reported numbers reproduce; nothing in the pre-registration is contradicted
findings.evidence: writer1/2/3.json and wordings.json sha256 match the pre-registration (aa94fbeb…, 241d892c…, e55ee4cf…, 3ec6d777…), and committed wordings.json equals blind5/wordings.json. One wording was replaced (writer 2's ticket_link/assignee, by writer 3's). plan_lessons_v13.json sha256 is 64cf5b30…, and it differs from v11's (f51b0b1b…) only in 'orders': true. There are no cie/src changes between e7b7530 and 949df2e. mdord/questions.jsonl was written at 00:35:59, after the freeze commit at 00:32:23. Recomputed with measure(): v11 0.667 to v13 1.000 on the action items. Only the 6 action-item answers differ between v11 and v13, with no plan-only differences elsewhere. v13 is right for the right reason (owner -> assignee_of -> label -> list) on all 8 in every folder. ROOM = 0.85, so rules 1 and 3 were measurable. The earlier-set means match the pre-registration's table.
findings.implication: The headline result stands as reported: 7 rules met, a +0.333 gain on the action items, and no change outside them. The write-up's limits should come from the scope findings above, not from protocol problems.
